main.title: Dance Dance Revolution
main.subtitle: The body becomes the controller
main.summary: Konami made rhythm visible on a floor of arrows, with performance spilling into the surrounding room.

cards.heading: Learning with the whole body
cards.text: Dance Dance Revolution arrived in Japanese arcades in 1998. Players matched foot movements to music and scrolling cues, learning patterns through their whole body rather than only through a joystick.

cards.heading: The arcade becomes a stage
cards.text: The cabinet made skill visible to spectators. Players could rehearse, improvise and perform together, turning an arcade into a temporary stage. Its popularity is a reminder that videogame history includes physical exertion and shared public space.

cards.heading: From Japan to Dancing Stage
cards.text: It was originally released to arcades in Japan on September 26, 1998. In March 1999, the game was released to North American arcades as Dance Dance Revolution and to European arcades under the name Dancing Stage.

cards.heading: Following the rhythm
cards.text: Players must step to the beat, matching the arrows presented to them on screen by stepping on arrows on a dance pad. Arrows come from the bottom to the top towards a set of stationary arrows known as the "Step Zone". If they reach it, players step on the pad and the game will then judge the accuracy of the timing, ranging from "Perfect", "Great", "Good", "Boo", to "Miss". An on-screen life meter, known as the Dance Gauge, begins halfway full at the start of each song. Perfect and Great steps slowly fill the Gauge, while Boo and Miss steps quickly deplete it. Good steps have no effect either way. If a player accumulates too many Boos or Misses, and the Dance Gauge becomes empty, the song fails and the game ends. The game also tracks a combo tally from 4 combos upward, which will break if players score Good or lower.

cards.heading: Reading a performance
cards.text: At the end of each song, players see their accumulated points, bonus points, and how many of each kind of step they made. They also get a letter grade that is dependent on the judgments received during play, ranging from SS, all steps Perfect, to E, failure, which is only seen in Couple mode when the other player passes. If players manage to pass all their songs a cumulative results screen is given, totaling the stats from all played stages.

main.title: Dynamite Cop
main.summary: A hijacked cruise ship becomes a supply of improvised weapons in a two-player brawl that keeps changing the next room.

cards.heading: The game
cards.text: Dynamite Cop is Sega AM1's 1998 Model 2 arcade beat'em-up, released in Japan as Dynamite Deka 2 and brought to Dreamcast in 1999. It follows Die Hard Arcade's fighting system into a rescue on a hijacked cruise ship and pirate island. Up to two players choose from three officers and use the scenery as readily as their fists.

cards.heading: Use what the room gives you
cards.text: A room's loose objects can become weapons. Chairs, bottles and stranger items give a brief advantage, while guns add a limited supply of shots to a close-range fight. Picking something up changes the next attack and encourages another look around the room when it is gone. The scenery is therefore more than a backdrop. A useful object near a group of enemies can change the approach, turning a crowded encounter into an opportunity for an improvised hit.

cards.heading: Keep the pair in the fight
cards.text: Punches, kicks and throws remain useful when the available weapons run out. Moving around the room helps keep enemies from surrounding an officer, and a second player adds another position from which to interrupt an attack. The pair shares the same small encounter space, so chasing a target also affects where the partner can fight. A brief opening can be used to finish one opponent, collect a weapon or get clear of the group closing in.

cards.heading: An interruption can change the route
cards.text: Short action sequences interrupt the brawling with a prompt to react at the right moment. The response can affect how the officers enter the next situation, giving a transition its own small test. Choosing an approach to the ship also changes the route through the rescue. Those shifts keep the next room from being a purely predictable succession: the player moves between direct fights, sudden reactions and another search for whatever the surrounding scene can turn into a weapon.

main.title: Mario Party
main.subtitle: An invitation to compete
main.summary: Mario Party is Hudson Soft's 1998 Nintendo 64 party game for up to four players. Mario and his friends compete across colourful boards, interrupting their journey with short minigames. Coins and Stars turn each small victory into something that can affect the longer contest.

cards.heading: An invitation to compete
cards.text: Mario Party is Hudson Soft's 1998 Nintendo 64 party game for up to four players. Mario and his friends compete across colourful boards, interrupting their journey with short minigames. Coins and Stars turn each small victory into something that can affect the longer contest.

cards.heading: The next roll
cards.text: Rolling a die moves a character around the board. A junction asks where to go next, while the space at the end can bring a reward, a loss or an event. The other players keep changing the situation before the next turn arrives. A promising position can become less comfortable without the character moving at all.

cards.heading: Partners for a moment
cards.text: The minigames repeatedly rearrange the competition. Everyone may compete alone, two players may become partners, or three may oppose a single rival. A player who helps someone win a team game still competes against them on the board. Quick explanations and short rounds let those temporary alliances form and dissolve throughout the match.

cards.heading: Watching the whole board
cards.text: Different boards give the contest another setting and different surprises. Hidden dangers make the route worth watching even during someone else's turn. The shared television keeps every reaction visible: a narrow escape or a sudden loss belongs to the whole room, including the people who benefit from it.

main.title: StarCraft
main.subtitle: From a strategy game to a spectator culture
main.summary: Blizzard's asymmetrical armies became part of a much larger competitive ecosystem, particularly in South Korea.

cards.heading: Three forces and continuing study
cards.text: StarCraft set three distinct forces against one another, requiring players to manage production, information and movement at once. Its multiplayer depth made learning an ongoing activity rather than something completed by finishing a campaign.

cards.heading: The places around competitive play
cards.text: In South Korea, PC rooms, organised competition and broadcasts helped make the game a public spectacle. Places to play, network infrastructure, commentators and audiences all helped build the competitive culture around it.

features.title: A room for playing and watching
features.summary: Watching and playing share a room.

cards.heading: Watching before learning to play
cards.text: Kook Kibong, known as TheBOy, recalled finding his friends playing StarCraft in an Australian internet café in 1998. He returned to watch before beginning to play himself. In Blizzard's later interview, he also remembered competing on Daytona USA machines and studying how to improve lap times. Watching other players was part of his introduction to competition.

cards.heading: Practice becomes a public life
cards.text: Kibong described building a reputation on Battle.net, gaining a manager and sponsor, and preparing strategies through repeated games and written notes. His memories of Korea's 1999 competitive scene included television appearances and a first live tournament. Practice and studying opponents became part of a professional career performed before an audience.

cards.heading: A room hosts a launch
cards.text: For a 2017 StarCraft: Remastered preview in Korea, Blizzard invited adult players to Gameinus's Sinnonhyeon PC bang in Seoul. The event combined a broadcast of the launch with overnight play, individual and team tournaments, and invited broadcaster matches. Spectators and participants could move between watching the presentation and playing in the same venue.

cards.heading: The place changes the programme
cards.text: The preview required registration, with limited places allocated by lottery and identification checked at the venue. Free overnight access formed part of the promotion. Because the programme ran beyond the hours when minors could enter, attendance was restricted to adults. These arrangements set the practical conditions for a shared evening of matches and broadcasts.

main.title: Blazing Star
main.subtitle: Six ships against a cybernetic army
main.summary: Blazing Star is Yumekobo's Neo Geo shooter, first released in Japanese arcades on 19 January 1998.

cards.heading: Six ships against a cybernetic army
cards.text: Blazing Star is Yumekobo's Neo Geo shooter, first released in Japanese arcades on 19 January 1998. Cyborg pilots turn against the artificial systems that created their armies, flying ships with different weapons and handling. The player chooses a craft before entering the side-scrolling stages, giving the journey an immediate personal variation. Large enemies and elaborate bosses fill the route, while the selected ship changes how much of the screen can be threatened and where it is safest to position an attack.

cards.heading: Charge a shot and choose its shape
cards.text: Tapping, rapidly pressing or holding the fire button produces different attacks. A charged shot can be released as a concentrated strike or dispersed across a wider area, and its behavior depends on the craft. The player can therefore change the shape of the attack to suit a formation or boss rather than relying only on movement. Different combinations of speed and firepower give each ship a distinct relationship with the same stage, making another choice of pilot a practical reason to learn the route again.

cards.heading: A brighter follow-up to Pulstar
cards.text: The game followed Aicom's Pulstar after the studio became Yumekobo. It aimed for a more approachable challenge while developing the pre-rendered visual style and dramatic boss presentation. Harumi Fujita composed the soundtrack. SNK published both the arcade game and its AES home release, which followed in February 1998. Blazing Star carries a recognizable Neo Geo spectacle into the later years of the hardware, using ship variety and flexible attacks to provide different ways through an otherwise fixed sequence of scrolling encounters.

main.title: Resident Evil 2
main.subtitle: Leon and Claire face the same catastrophe
main.summary: Capcom released Biohazard 2 for PlayStation in Japan on January 29, 1998, eight days after Resident Evil 2's North American debut.

cards.heading: Surviving Raccoon City
cards.text: Capcom released Biohazard 2 for PlayStation in Japan on January 29, 1998, eight days after Resident Evil 2's North American debut. Leon S. Kennedy and Claire Redfield arrive in a Raccoon City overrun by disaster. Streets, the police station, sewers and laboratories form their routes through it. Limited ammunition and inventory space keep pressure on the player, while connected scenarios reveal different parts of the catastrophe.

cards.heading: The outbreak reaches the streets
cards.text: The outbreak moves survival horror from an isolated mansion into a city. Raccoon City's streets lead to dense interiors that require keys, orientation and repeated visits. Offices, public buildings and homes give the disaster a wider setting. Leon and Claire encounter a community already collapsing, gradually discovering how its different locations connect.

cards.heading: Finding routes through the R.P.D.
cards.text: The Raccoon Police Department forms the centre of the maze. Once a museum, it retains grand staircases, statues and elaborate corridors alongside police desks, cells and offices. As players return with keys and solve mechanisms, shortcuts reveal the building's layout. Routes eventually lead beneath the station toward the sewers and Umbrella's laboratories.

cards.heading: Leon, Claire and the B scenarios
cards.text: One disc follows Leon, a police officer arriving for his first day; the other follows Claire as she searches for her brother Chris. They meet different people and use different weapons. Completing an initial scenario opens a B scenario for the other character, with variations connected to the chosen order. The zapping system allows some actions in one route to affect the other.

main.title: Fighters Destiny
main.subtitle: Genki / Opus / Anchor · Nintendo 64
main.summary: Fighters Destiny is a Nintendo 64 fighting game whose matches award points for different kinds of victory. A ring-out, throw or knockout can each contribute a different amount toward the total needed to win. The system makes the current score part of deciding how to approach an opponent. A modest opportunity may be enough to finish a match, while another situation makes a riskier technique worthwhile. Punches, kicks and movement remain familiar, but the value of their result changes with the way the exchange ends.

cards.heading: Win the fight through points as well as damage
cards.text: Fighters Destiny is a Nintendo 64 fighting game whose matches award points for different kinds of victory. A ring-out, throw or knockout can each contribute a different amount toward the total needed to win. The system makes the current score part of deciding how to approach an opponent. A modest opportunity may be enough to finish a match, while another situation makes a riskier technique worthwhile. Punches, kicks and movement remain familiar, but the value of their result changes with the way the exchange ends.

cards.heading: A depleted gauge is another opening
cards.text: Reducing an opponent's health can leave them briefly dizzy, creating a chance to deliver a finishing move. Surviving that condition allows the fighter to recover, so an advantage has to be converted into a useful result. The arena boundary provides another possible route to points, making position important alongside the current health. The player has to recognise whether to pursue damage, a throw or a push toward the edge. The next successful action matters because of what it completes, not simply how much of the gauge it removes.

cards.heading: Develop the fighter between matches
cards.text: Additional modes provide challenges and ways to acquire moves, with a Controller Pak able to preserve an expanded command list. Training against a robot gives space to learn the next technique before using it against another person. Released in 1998, the game was known in Japan as Fighting Cup and later received a sequel. Its strongest idea is the scoring structure: several kinds of successful exchange remain useful, giving two familiar-looking fighters more than one practical reason to change their approach during a match.

main.title: Panzer Dragoon Saga
main.summary: Edge and his dragon explore an ancient world in a role-playing adventure whose battles turn timing and position into tactical decisions.

cards.heading: The game
cards.text: Panzer Dragoon Saga is a role-playing game developed by Sega's Team Andromeda for Sega Saturn. Released in 1998, it is the third Panzer Dragoon game, known in Japan as Azel: Panzer Dragoon RPG. It expands the series' world through exploration on foot, dragon flight and battles fought around a moving enemy.

cards.heading: A world beyond the flight path
cards.text: After surviving an attack on an excavation site, the young mercenary Edge sets out with a dragon to find the soldiers responsible. Ruins and settlements give that pursuit a world to move through. Flying lets him search broad areas and use the dragon's lasers to break obstacles; landing brings conversations, shops and discoveries at close range. A targeting cursor serves both kinds of exploration, picking out a person to speak to, an object to inspect or a barrier to destroy.

cards.heading: Circle, wait, strike
cards.text: In battle, Edge and the dragon can move between positions around an opponent. The radar marks the danger on each side, so exposing a weak point may also mean entering the path of a stronger attack. Three gauges fill while the fight continues; charged gauges pay for shots, items and the dragon's special abilities. Moving interrupts that charge. The decision is immediate: stay where it is safer and build up actions, or reposition now to seize an opening before the enemy changes course.

cards.heading: A dragon shaped for the next battle
cards.text: The dragon's form can be adjusted in the Type Select screen. Moving the cursor changes its balance of attack, defence, agility and spiritual power, and its body changes with those choices. A faster form helps the action gauges recover, while another favours the homing laser or the special attacks called Berserks. These are ways of preparing for a particular encounter: a useful shape for one enemy can give up a strength needed against the next. The companion is also the player's most flexible piece of equipment.

main.title: Skullmonkeys
main.subtitle: Klaymen trades puzzles for platforms
main.summary: Skullmonkeys is The Neverhood, Inc.'s PlayStation platform game, first released in North America on 6 February 1998. Klaymen returns from The Neverhood to confront creatures controlled by his old enemy Klogg, but the earlier adventure's pointing and clicking gives way to running and jumping. Sculpted clay characters and scenery retain the world's handmade appearance. The player moves through a succession of strange places whose humour often arrives through a face, sound or unexpected movement. Its identity comes as much from how those objects were made as from the route through each level.

cards.heading: Klaymen trades puzzles for platforms
cards.text: Skullmonkeys is The Neverhood, Inc.'s PlayStation platform game, first released in North America on 6 February 1998. Klaymen returns from The Neverhood to confront creatures controlled by his old enemy Klogg, but the earlier adventure's pointing and clicking gives way to running and jumping. Sculpted clay characters and scenery retain the world's handmade appearance. The player moves through a succession of strange places whose humour often arrives through a face, sound or unexpected movement. Its identity comes as much from how those objects were made as from the route through each level.

cards.heading: Jump first, then use the stranger tools
cards.text: Klaymen can defeat enemies by landing on them, while collected weapons offer other ways to remove a threat. A halo allows him to survive an additional hit, making the next mistake less final. Secret areas provide bonus points and extra lives, rewarding attention to the edges of the main route. The side-scrolling structure keeps the task clear even when the world becomes increasingly absurd. The player reads a familiar platforming problem through unfamiliar materials, with clay figures and deliberately odd details giving a conventional jump a different personality.

cards.heading: A soundtrack as unusual as the scenery
cards.text: Terry Scott Taylor composed music that supports the game's comic and unsettling atmosphere, including deliberately relaxed material for its bonus stages. The same commitment to a particular tone connects Skullmonkeys to The Neverhood despite the change of genre. Reviews praised the clay-based appearance and music while finding less variety in the underlying play. The European release followed in February 1998. The game remains a distinctive PlayStation object because its visual world appears physically constructed, preserving the marks of a craft process inside a machine associated with the arrival of three-dimensional graphics.

main.title: James Bond 007
main.subtitle: Saffire · Game Boy
main.summary: James Bond 007 is Saffire's Game Boy action adventure about a weapons-smuggling operation that grows into a much larger threat. The agent travels through villages, cities and hostile facilities, meeting familiar film characters including Oddjob and Jaws. Viewed from above, the journey makes room for conversation, exploration and the use of collected objects between fights. A new location can ask Bond to find information or a useful tool before confronting its guards, giving the portable mission a different rhythm from the first-person action associated with GoldenEye.

cards.heading: Bond investigates from above
cards.text: James Bond 007 is Saffire's Game Boy action adventure about a weapons-smuggling operation that grows into a much larger threat. The agent travels through villages, cities and hostile facilities, meeting familiar film characters including Oddjob and Jaws. Viewed from above, the journey makes room for conversation, exploration and the use of collected objects between fights. A new location can ask Bond to find information or a useful tool before confronting its guards, giving the portable mission a different rhythm from the first-person action associated with GoldenEye.

cards.heading: The right item opens the next part of the mission
cards.text: Bond carries weapons and other equipment whose purpose depends on the situation. Some problems require an object to be used at the appropriate place, while others can be handled through fists, martial arts or gunfire. The player has to investigate the surroundings rather than assume every obstacle is another target. Eleven levels provide the route through the conspiracy, with casino games such as baccarat and blackjack adding another familiar part of the agent's world. The changing tasks give a small overhead figure several recognisably Bond-like roles.

cards.heading: A different Bond for a different Nintendo machine
cards.text: Nintendo published the game in 1998, following the enormous success of GoldenEye on Nintendo 64. Saffire built an original portable adventure rather than attempt to reproduce that console game's perspective. Super Game Boy support added colour when played through the television accessory, while cartridge saves preserved the longer mission between sessions. The result expresses the licence through the breadth of an assignment: travel, talk, gamble, investigate and fight all belong to the same journey, allowing the handheld to represent more than a series of shooting encounters.
